source.title: Tripartite: Tackle Noisy Labels by a More Precise Partition
source.authors: Xue-Feng Liang; Longshan Yao; Xingyu Liu; Ying Zhou

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests training under randomly corrupted labels and reports Standard CE test accuracy, but does not measure whether training error reaches zero.
record.gate_note: Only Standard CE test-accuracy results under symmetric label noise bear on V4. The other reported results concern the proposed noisy-label method, data partitioning, or cited methods; they do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Tripartite uses the premise that networks learn shared patterns before memorizing noisy labels to design a mitigation method. Its own results measure mitigation and partitioning performance. The Standard CE values in Table 1 are explicitly borrowed from reference [18], DivideMix, rather than measured in this study.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Tripartite improves partition quality and outperforms most compared methods across noisy-label benchmarks, especially real-world datasets. They acknowledge weaker performance than leading methods at 80% symmetric noise.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies noisy-label learning with an 18-layer PreAct Resnet and SGD; the Standard CE comparator is trained on corrupted-label datasets. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy varies with the symmetric noise ratio and dataset; these results do not establish training-error behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Tripartite improves noisy-label partitioning and classification performance using separate learning strategies for clean, hard, and noisy subsets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Partitioning noisy training data into three subsets can improve noisy-label mitigation relative to the compared methods.

record.problems: For the claim-relevant Standard CE results, only test accuracy is reported; training error, chance-level test error, and results at 100% corruption are absent. Table 1 reports averages of 5 trials for experiments, without uncertainty for these entries.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly measure any claim version. Table 1 results for methods other than Standard CE, and results for Tripartite's own method, address noisy-label method performance rather than the claim's standard-network fitting behavior.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The study provides no own standard-network sweep establishing perfect training fitting alongside steadily worsening test error. Its mitigation results do not measure memorization of the corrupted labels.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.

Direct comparison of learning shared real-label patterns versus memorizing noisy labels over training. Section 3.1 adopts this premise from prior studies; partition statistics and normalized-loss distributions do not establish that temporal sequence.

record.verdict_notes: Remove R1–R6 as own-study evidence: Table 1's caption attributes these Standard CE results to [18]. Their declining accuracy across noise levels is cited evidence only. No verdict follows from these rows.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling experiment or training-error result.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed for true versus random labels.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.

The paper reports test accuracy under 20%, 50%, and 80% symmetric noise, but not training error, perfect fitting, a sweep from none to all labels corrupted, or whether remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized.
No random-label experiment testing weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation, and no corresponding true-label generalization comparison.
No measurement of whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.
